title: They Gathered Information, They Monitored: the Examiner on Repo 105 and the Regulators Who Watched
participants: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The quantity is in the Examiner's Report as read into the hearing record: "although Lehman had in effect borrowed tens of billions of dollars in these transactions, Lehman did not disclose the known obligation to repay the debt."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was an accounting characterisation. "Lehman employed off-balance sheet devices known within Lehman as 'Repo 105' and 'Repo 108' transactions to temporarily remove securities inventory from its balance sheet, usually for a period of 7 to 10 days ... Lehman accounted for Repo 105 transactions as sales as opposed to financing transactions. By recharacterizing the Repo 105 transaction as a sale, Lehman removed the inventory from its balance sheet." Seven to ten days, timed: "Lehman regularly increased its use of Repo 105 transactions in the days prior to the reporting periods."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The Examiner's word for it is engineering. "In this way, unbeknownst to the investing public, rating agencies, government regulators, and Lehman's board of directors, Lehman reverse engineered the firm's net leverage ratio for public consumption." Inside the firm it was understood as what it was: "A senior member of Lehman's financial group considered Lehman's Repo 105 program to be balance sheet 'window dressing' that was based on legal technicalities. Other former Lehman employees characterized Repo 105 transactions as an accounting gimmick and a lazy way of managing the balance sheet."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The benefit was a rating, and the Report states the stake: "Starting in mid-2007, Lehman faced a crisis. Marked observers began demanding that investment banks reduce their leverage. The inability to reduce leverage could lead to a ratings downgrade, which would have had an immediate, tangible monetary impact on Lehman." The Examiner's conclusion is categorical: "Repo 105 transactions were not used for a business purpose, but instead for an accounting purpose: to reduce Lehman's publicly reported net leverage and net balance sheet." And the device required the concealment to work: "In order for this off-balance sheet device to benefit Lehman, the firm had to conceal information regarding its Repo 105 practice from the public."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The watching is the stage, and the Examiner testified to it in detail. "By at least 2007, various agencies of the United States Government were concerned at the highest levels with the prospects for Lehman's survival. The concerns did not translate into action. Governing agencies gathered information, they monitored, but no agency effectively regulated or compelled Lehman to alter its conduct." The Report puts monitors inside the building: "The day after Bear Stearns Weekend, teams of government monitors from the SEC and the Federal Reserve Board New York were dispatched to and took up residence at Lehman to review and monitor its financial situation." And the specific failures are itemised: the SEC knew in 2007 that Lehman "persistently exceeded its internal risk limits" and "never required that Lehman take steps to reduce its risk profile nor did it require Lehman to disclose that it was in breach of its limits. So that was never publicly disclosed to rating agencies or anyone else." It knew by June 2008 that encumbered assets were being counted in the liquidity pool and "did not require any action by Lehman, nor did they make any public disclosure of that."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The SEC's voluntary Consolidated Supervised Entity programme, under which the SEC was "Lehman's primary regulator", and a division of labour the Examiner describes as structurally broken: "The Federal Reserve Bank of New York gathered and analyzed information from Lehman, but it viewed its role as a potential lender and not as a regulator, and it deferred to the SEC."
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: This hearing is itself the mechanism — "Public Policy Issues Raised by the Report of the Lehman Bankruptcy Examiner" — and the diagnosis it produced is the one the Examiner stated: "The agency, with the skill sets to regulate a financial institution like Lehman, which might be the Fed, did not have the authority, and the agency with the authority, the SEC, may not have possessed the skill set."
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Leverage must fall or the rating falls; the rating falling costs real money; so leverage is removed from the reported balance sheet for seven to ten days around each reporting date; the reported figure reassures the rating agencies, the regulators and the firm's own board; the reassurance permits the position to grow; and the regulators watching never ask the one question that would show it, because, as the Examiner put it, "it did not ask the right questions. Its failure to ask about off-balance sheet transactions in this post-Enron era is hard to understand."

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the government let Lehman fail on purpose — that a decision was taken to sacrifice one bank, and that had the regulators acted, the firm and the crisis could have been avoided.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Examiner refused that reading in his own testimony, and his refusal is the most useful paragraph in the record: "I must emphasize, as I attempted to set out in the report, that Lehman's failure was the result of many factors. There is no single cause or actor involved here. There is no bright line action that can be said in retrospect, had the government done this, Lehman would not have failed. It is far from clear that the most engaged regulator could have saved Lehman from its fate. But what is clear is had the government acted sooner on what it did know or should have known, there would have been more opportunities to spare the markets and the American people the turmoil of Lehman's abrupt failure." That is both halves at once, from the person who spent a year with the documents: no single cause, no saving action — and yet a knowledge asymmetry that was real and dated. The agencies "recognized as early as 2007, but certainly by mid-March 2008 ... that Lehman could fail"; Paulson, Bernanke, Geithner and Cox all had direct communication with Lehman's chief executive; monitors from the SEC and the New York Fed "took up residence at Lehman" the day after Bear Stearns Weekend. Meanwhile the SEC knew of persistent risk-limit breaches it never required to be disclosed "to rating agencies or anyone else", and knew by June 2008 that the liquidity pool contained encumbered assets and made no public disclosure of that either. The two agencies that each held half the picture "failed to share certain information with each other". The Examiner's phrase for the whole posture is the one to keep: "although the public had a right to expect that firms like Lehman were being regulated in a meaningful way, in reality, they were not." A STATED LIMIT ON THIS DOSSIER'S SOURCE: the Examiner's Report itself has NOT been read. It is published at jenner.com, which serves a bot-verification interstitial that was not circumvented. What was read is the congressional hearing on it, containing the Examiner's sworn testimony and verbatim quotations from the Report with page citations — and every quotation above is marked as one or the other. No criminal or civil proceeding against any Lehman officer was read, and none is asserted.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The hearing "Public Policy Issues Raised by the Report of the Lehman Bankruptcy Examiner" before the House Committee on Financial Services, 20 April 2010, Serial No. 111-124. It contains verbatim quotations from the Examiner's Report at pages 732, 733, 735, 738, 739, 742–743, 746, 853 and 1,482–1,483 recording: Repo 105 and Repo 108 as off-balance sheet devices removing securities inventory for seven to ten days to create a materially misleading picture of the firm's condition in late 2007 and 2008, accounted for as sales rather than financings; their use increased in the days before reporting periods, with tens of billions borrowed and the obligation to repay undisclosed; the mid-2007 pressure to reduce leverage and the monetary consequence of a downgrade; the firm having "reverse engineered" its net leverage ratio for public consumption, unbeknownst to the investing public, rating agencies, regulators and its own board; internal descriptions as "window dressing", an accounting gimmick and a lazy way of managing the balance sheet; the conclusion that the transactions served no business purpose but an accounting one; the necessity of concealment for the device to work; and the agencies' recognition as early as 2007, and certainly by mid-March 2008, that Lehman could fail, with direct communication between Paulson, Bernanke, Geithner and Cox and Lehman's former chief executive and SEC and New York Fed monitors taking up residence at the firm after Bear Stearns Weekend. It also contains the Examiner's own testimony that the public had a right to expect meaningful regulation and did not get it; that concerns at the highest levels did not translate into action; that the New York Fed saw itself as a potential lender rather than a regulator and deferred to the SEC; that the SEC knew of persistent internal risk-limit breaches in 2007 and required neither reduction nor disclosure, so that nothing was disclosed to rating agencies or anyone else, and that the inability to liquidate assets acquired in breach of those limits contributed to the collapse; that the SEC knew by June 2008 of encumbered assets counted in the liquidity pool and required no action and made no disclosure; that it did not know about Repo 105 because it did not ask the right questions; that the SEC and the New York Fed each held knowledge the other lacked and did not combine it; that the agency with the skills lacked the authority and the agency with the authority may have lacked the skills; and that the failure had many causes, with no single cause or actor and no bright-line action that would have prevented it.

WHY THIS DOCUMENT AND NOT THE EXAMINER'S REPORT: the Report itself is published at jenner.com, which serves a bot-verification interstitial that was NOT circumvented, so the Report has not been read. What has been read is the congressional hearing on it, which contains the Examiner's own sworn testimony and verbatim quotations from the Report with page citations. Everything below is either Anton R. Valukas speaking, or a Member reading the Report into the record — and which it is, is marked. QUOTED FROM THE REPORT BY A MEMBER, with the Report's page numbers as given in the hearing. Page 732: "Lehman employed off-balance sheet devices known within Lehman as 'Repo 105' and 'Repo 108' transactions to temporarily remove securities inventory from its balance sheet, usually for a period of 7 to 10 days, and to create a materially misleading picture of the firm's financial condition in late 2007 and 2008. Lehman accounted for Repo 105 transactions as sales as opposed to financing transactions. By recharacterizing the Repo 105 transaction as a sale, Lehman removed the inventory from its balance sheet." Page 733: "Lehman regularly increased its use of Repo 105 transactions in the days prior to the reporting periods to reduce its publicly reported net leverage and balance sheet. Lehman's periodic reports did not disclose the cash borrowing from the Repo 105 transaction; i.e., although Lehman had in effect borrowed tens of billions of dollars in these transactions, Lehman did not disclose the known obligation to repay the debt." Page 735: "Starting in mid-2007, Lehman faced a crisis. Marked observers began demanding that investment banks reduce their leverage. The inability to reduce leverage could lead to a ratings downgrade, which would have had an immediate, tangible monetary impact on Lehman." Page 739: "In this way, unbeknownst to the investing public, rating agencies, government regulators, and Lehman's board of directors, Lehman reverse engineered the firm's net leverage ratio for public consumption." Pages 742–743: "A senior member of Lehman's financial group considered Lehman's Repo 105 program to be balance sheet 'window dressing' that was based on legal technicalities. Other former Lehman employees characterized Repo 105 transactions as an accounting gimmick and a lazy way of managing the balance sheet." Page 746: "Repo 105 transactions were not used for a business purpose, but instead for an accounting purpose: to reduce Lehman's publicly reported net leverage and net balance sheet." Page 853: "In order for this off-balance sheet device to benefit Lehman, the firm had to conceal information regarding its Repo 105 practice from the public." Pages 1,482–1,483: "At the highest levels, each of these agencies recognized as early as 2007, but certainly by mid-March 2008, after the Bear Stearns near collapse, that Lehman could fail. Treasury Secretary Paulson, Federal Chairman Bernanke, the Federal Reserve Board New York Secretary Geithner, and SEC Chairman Cox all had direct communication with former Lehman CEO Fuld. The day after Bear Stearns Weekend, teams of government monitors from the SEC and the Federal Reserve Board New York were dispatched to and took up residence at Lehman to review and monitor its financial situation." THE EXAMINER'S OWN TESTIMONY, which is the better part of this record. "First, although the public had a right to expect that firms like Lehman were being regulated in a meaningful way, in reality, they were not." "By at least 2007, various agencies of the United States Government were concerned at the highest levels with the prospects for Lehman's survival. The concerns did not translate into action. Governing agencies gathered information, they monitored, but no agency effectively regulated or compelled Lehman to alter its conduct. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York gathered and analyzed information from Lehman, but it viewed its role as a potential lender and not as a regulator, and it deferred to the SEC." On the SEC: "the SEC knew in 2007 that Lehman persistently exceeded its internal risk limits, limits that they had been told initially were hard limits and that would not be exceeded ... The SEC never required that Lehman take steps to reduce its risk profile nor did it require Lehman to disclose that it was in breach of its limits. So that was never publicly disclosed to rating agencies or anyone else. The inability of Lehman to liquidate some of these same assets in 2008, the assets which they acquired in breach of these risk limits, was, in fact, a contributing factor to Lehman's demise." "The SEC knew as early as June of 2008 that Lehman was reporting sums in its liquidity pool that the SEC determined were not, in fact, appropriately within that pool because they were encumbered, but the SEC did not require any action by Lehman, nor did they make any public disclosure of that. The SEC did not know that Lehman was manipulating its balance sheet to make its leverage appear better than it was by using repo 105 transactions that I describe in detail in my report. The SEC did not know this because it did not ask the right questions. Its failure to ask about off-balance sheet transactions in this post-Enron era is hard to understand." On the two agencies: "the SEC and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York failed to share certain information with each other about Lehman's liquidity and Lehman's inclusion of encumbered assets in its liquidity pool. Each agency had knowledge not possessed by the other. Had they combined that knowledge, they would have realized earlier the severity of Lehman's liquidity position when there was still possibly time to do something to at least to soften the fall." And: "The agency, with the skill sets to regulate a financial institution like Lehman, which might be the Fed, did not have the authority, and the agency with the authority, the SEC, may not have possessed the skill set." THE EXAMINER'S OWN REFUSAL OF A SINGLE-CAUSE ACCOUNT, quoted in full because it is the most important paragraph for this dossier: "I must emphasize, as I attempted to set out in the report, that Lehman's failure was the result of many factors. There is no single cause or actor involved here. There is no bright line action that can be said in retrospect, had the government done this, Lehman would not have failed. It is far from clear that the most engaged regulator could have saved Lehman from its fate. But what is clear is had the government acted sooner on what it did know or should have known, there would have been more opportunities to spare the markets and the American people the turmoil of Lehman's abrupt failure. What is clear is that the regulators were not fully engaged and did not direct Lehman to alter the conduct which we now know in retrospect led to Lehman's ruin."
